title: UNIT 1: VECTOR QUANTITIES
notes:
✓ Physical quantity → A number or set of numbers used to describe a physical phenomenon.

✓ Physical quantities → Are classified as scalars or vectors.

◆ CORE IDEA
✓ Scalar → Has magnitude only.
✓ Vector → Has both magnitude and direction.

✓ Vectors → Are essential for describing physical quantities such as displacement, velocity, acceleration and force because their directions affect physical results.

title: 1.1 SCALARS AND VECTORS
notes:
✓ Physical quantities → Can be completely described in two different ways.

◆ SCALAR QUANTITY
✓ Scalar → A physical quantity completely specified by a numerical value and an appropriate unit; it has magnitude only.

◆ Examples
Time • distance • speed • length • volume • temperature • energy • power • mass • density.

◆ VECTOR QUANTITY
✓ Vector → A physical quantity that requires both magnitude and direction for complete description.

◆ Examples
Displacement • velocity • acceleration • force • momentum • impulse • weight • electric field strength.

◆ EXAMPLES
✓ Speed = 80 km/h → Complete scalar description.
✓ Velocity = 80 km/h East → Magnitude + direction.
✓ Force = 20 N → Incomplete vector description unless its direction is specified.

◆ KEY DIFFERENCE
✓ Scalar → Magnitude only.
✓ Vector → Magnitude + direction.

✓ Two physical quantities → Cannot be added as vectors unless they are quantities of the same physical type.

✓ Two forces or two velocities → Can be added.
✓ Force + velocity → Cannot be added.

title: 1.2 VECTOR REPRESENTATIONS
notes:
✓ Vectors → Can be represented algebraically or geometrically.

◆ ALGEBRAIC REPRESENTATION
✓ A vector → Can be written using a bold letter or an arrow over the letter:
A or A⃗

✓ Magnitude → Can be written as:
|A⃗| or A

✓ Example:
S⃗ = 50 km Southwest

✓ 50 km → Magnitude.
✓ Southwest → Direction.

◆ GEOMETRICAL REPRESENTATION
✓ Vector → Is represented by an arrow or arrow-tipped line segment.
✓ Tail → Initial point of the vector.
✓ Head → Final point/arrowhead.
✓ Arrow length → Represents magnitude when drawn to scale.
✓ Arrowhead → Represents direction.

◆ SCALE
✓ Vector diagram → Must use an appropriate scale.

✓ Example:
1 cm = 2 N

✓ A 20 N force → Is represented by an arrow 10 cm long.

◆ REFERENCE DIRECTION
✓ Reference direction → Must be specified, such as a horizontal line or compass directions (North, South, East and West).

◆ STEPS TO DRAW A VECTOR
✓ Choose and record a suitable scale.
✓ Determine the arrow length using the scale.
✓ Draw the arrow in the specified direction.
✓ Label the magnitude/vector.

✓ Important → A vector diagram should show both the magnitude and direction accurately.

title: 1.2 TYPES OF VECTORS
notes:
✓ Different types of vectors → Are classified according to their magnitude and direction.

◆ ZERO / NULL VECTOR
✓ Zero vector → A vector with zero magnitude and no definite direction.

A⃗ = 0

◆ UNIT VECTOR
✓ Unit vector → A vector whose magnitude is exactly one.

|A⃗| = 1

◆ EQUAL VECTORS
✓ Equal vectors → Have the same magnitude and the same direction.

A⃗ = B⃗

◆ NEGATIVE OF A VECTOR
✓ Negative vector → Has the same magnitude as the original vector but the opposite direction.

−A⃗

✓ |−A⃗| = |A⃗|

✓ Their directions → Are opposite.

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Equal vectors → Same magnitude + same direction.
✓ Negative vectors → Same magnitude + opposite direction.
✓ Zero vector → Zero magnitude.

title: 1.3 VECTOR ADDITION AND SUBTRACTION
notes:
✓ Vector addition → Combines two or more vectors to produce a single vector called the resultant.

◆ RESULTANT VECTOR
✓ Resultant → The single vector whose effect is the same as the combined effect of the individual vectors.

✓ For vectors A⃗ and B⃗:
R⃗ = A⃗ + B⃗

◆ VECTORS THAT CAN BE ADDED
✓ Only quantities of the same physical type → Can be added as vectors.

✓ Examples → Force + force; velocity + velocity.
✓ Force + velocity → Cannot be added.

◆ VECTOR ADDITION
✓ Vector addition → Must consider both magnitude and direction.

✓ Ordinary scalar addition → Cannot generally be used for vectors.

◆ VECTOR SUBTRACTION
✓ Vector subtraction → Is defined as addition of the negative vector.

A⃗ − B⃗ = A⃗ + (−B⃗)

✓ To subtract B⃗ from A⃗:
✓ Reverse B⃗ → Obtain −B⃗.
✓ Add −B⃗ to A⃗ → Use the appropriate vector-addition method.

✓ Key idea → Subtraction of a vector = addition of its negative.

title: 1.3 RESULTANT OF TWO VECTORS
notes:
✓ Resultant magnitude → Depends on the relative directions of the vectors.

◆ SAME DIRECTION
✓ If two vectors point in the same direction:
R = A + B

◆ OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS
✓ If two vectors point in opposite directions:
R = |A − B|

✓ Resultant → Points in the direction of the larger vector.

◆ PERPENDICULAR VECTORS
✓ If two vectors are at 90°:
R = √(A² + B²)

◆ RANGE OF RESULTANT
✓ For two vectors with magnitudes A and B:

✓ Maximum resultant = A + B
✓ Minimum resultant = |A − B|

✓ Important → The direction between vectors determines the magnitude and direction of their resultant.

title: 1.4 GRAPHICAL METHOD OF VECTOR ADDITION
notes:
✓ Vectors → Can be added or subtracted graphically.

✓ Vectors → Are drawn to scale and the resultant is determined using a ruler and protractor.

◆ METHODS
✓ Triangle method.
✓ Parallelogram method.
✓ Polygon method.

◆ GENERAL PROCEDURE
✓ Choose an appropriate scale and record it.
✓ Pick a starting point.
✓ Draw the first vector to scale in its indicated direction.
✓ Draw the remaining vector(s) with correct magnitude and direction.
✓ Draw the resultant according to the chosen method.
✓ Measure the resultant length with a ruler.
✓ Convert the measured length to magnitude using the scale.
✓ Measure the resultant direction using a protractor.

title: 1.4 TRIANGLE METHOD
notes:
✓ Triangle method → Also called the head-to-tail method and is used to add two vectors.

◆ PROCEDURE
✓ Draw the first vector.
✓ Place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector.
✓ Draw the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector.

✓ For vectors A⃗ and B⃗:
R⃗ = A⃗ + B⃗

◆ TRIANGLE LAW
✓ If two vectors acting simultaneously on a body are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in order → Their resultant is represented by the third side taken in the opposite order.

◆ HEAD-TO-TAIL RULE
✓ Tail of B⃗ → Placed at head of A⃗.
✓ Resultant → Tail of A⃗ to head of B⃗.

title: 1.4 PARALLELOGRAM METHOD
notes:
✓ Parallelogram method → Is used to find the resultant of two vectors acting from the same point.

◆ PROCEDURE
✓ Draw the two vectors from the same starting point.
✓ Draw a line parallel to the first vector through the head of the second.
✓ Draw a line parallel to the second vector through the head of the first.
✓ The vectors → Form a parallelogram.
✓ Draw the diagonal from the common tail to the opposite corner.

◆ RESULTANT
✓ Diagonal → Represents the resultant vector.

R⃗ = A⃗ + B⃗

◆ KEY IDEA
✓ Triangle method → Head-to-tail.
✓ Parallelogram method → Vectors start from the same point.

title: 1.4 POLYGON METHOD
notes:
✓ Polygon method → Is used to add more than two vectors.

◆ PROCEDURE
✓ Draw the first vector to scale.
✓ Place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first.
✓ Continue placing each vector head-to-tail.
✓ Draw the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the head of the final vector.

◆ RESULTANT
✓ Resultant → Represents the combined effect of all the vectors.

◆ SPECIAL CASE
✓ If vectors are added head-to-tail and the final vector ends at the starting point → The resultant is zero.

R⃗ = 0

✓ Closed vector polygon → A head-to-tail vector arrangement with zero resultant.

title: 1.5 VECTOR RESOLUTION
notes:
✓ Vector resolution → The process of breaking a single vector into component vectors whose vector sum equals the original vector.

✓ Component vectors → Are called components of the original vector.

◆ RECTANGULAR COMPONENTS
✓ A vector A⃗ → Can be resolved into:

A⃗x → Horizontal component along the x-axis.

A⃗y → Vertical component along the y-axis.

✓ Original vector → Is the sum of its components:
A⃗ = A⃗x + A⃗y

✓ Perpendicular components → Form a right triangle with the original vector as the hypotenuse.

✓ Key idea → Vector addition combines vectors into a resultant.
✓ Vector resolution → Breaks one vector into components.

title: 1.5 GRAPHICAL METHOD OF VECTOR RESOLUTION
notes:
✓ A vector → Can be resolved graphically into horizontal and vertical components.

◆ PROCEDURE
✓ Select an appropriate scale.
✓ Draw the vector to scale in the correct direction.
✓ Extend the x- and y-axes from the vector's tail.
✓ From the arrowhead → Construct perpendicular projections to the x- and y-axes.
✓ Draw the x-component from the tail to the x-axis projection and label it A⃗x.
✓ Draw the y-component from the tail to the y-axis projection and label it A⃗y.
✓ Measure the component lengths and use the scale to determine their magnitudes.

◆ RESULT
A⃗ = A⃗x + A⃗y

title: 1.5 TRIGONOMETRIC METHOD OF VECTOR RESOLUTION
notes:
✓ If vector A⃗ makes an angle θ measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis → Its rectangular components are found using trigonometry.

◆ HORIZONTAL COMPONENT
✓ cos θ = Ax/A

✓ Ax = A cos θ

◆ VERTICAL COMPONENT
✓ sin θ = Ay/A

✓ Ay = A sin θ

◆ RESULTANT MAGNITUDE
✓ Since Ax and Ay are perpendicular:
A = √(Ax² + Ay²)

◆ DIRECTION
✓ The direction → Can be determined using:
tan θ = Ay/Ax

✓ Important → The signs of Ax and Ay depend on the quadrant/direction of the original vector.

title: 1.5 RESULTANT USING COMPONENTS
notes:
✓ When several vectors act together → Each vector can be resolved into x- and y-components.

◆ GENERAL IDEA
✓ Resolve each vector → Into horizontal and vertical components.
✓ Add all x-components.
✓ Add all y-components.
✓ Use the resulting x- and y-components → Determine the resultant magnitude and direction.

✓ If the total components are Rx and Ry:
R = √(Rx² + Ry²)

✓ Direction:
tan θ = Ry/Rx

✓ Key idea → Component method simplifies vector problems by treating perpendicular components separately.
